extracted.intended_audience: patent scholars, intellectual property lawyers, judges, and policymakers concerned with patent-eligibility (§101) issues in biotechnology
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly analysis of how Supreme Court jurisprudence (Myriad, Mayo, Chakrabarty, Funk Bros., Alice) and related doctrines bear on patent-eligibility of biological compositions (e.g., gDNA, cDNA) and on the conceptual relationship between products-of-nature and laws-of-nature exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws-of-nature / natural-phenomena / abstract-ideas exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: “Laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are not patentable.” (quotation from Mayo, cited in Myriad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this canonical §101 exception to screen process claims (e.g., diagnostic methods) and to motivate preemption concerns; the Court has repeatedly applied it to deny patents that effectively claim fundamental principles or causal correlations rather than their particular applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products-of-nature doctrine (existence and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court affirms that there is a discrete judicial doctrine excluding 'products of nature' from patentable subject matter (e.g., 'a new mineral discovered in the earth or a new plant found in the wild' may be excluded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that Myriad is the first Supreme Court case since post-1952 obviousness codification to squarely hold a material unpatentable as a product of nature; the doctrine's historical pedigree and scope are confused and contested, and lower courts must clarify how it operates in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural-alteration criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed molecule may be patent-eligible if its chemical structure is meaningfully altered from the naturally occurring counterpart (the Federal Circuit's rationale permitting cDNA-like claims because of structural change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether extraction or synthetic manipulation changes chemical structure (e.g., removal of introns in cDNA) and whether such structural changes are sufficiently distinct to support eligibility — noting the Supreme Court's ambiguous treatment of this rationale in Myriad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information/content sameness criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed molecule embodies the same nucleotide 'coding information' as the native molecule, it may be treated as a product of nature (Justice Thomas’s emphasis in Myriad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claim essentially captures the same informational template/process (coding sequence) as found in nature; be aware this approach conflicts with structural tests and produces indeterminate results when structure and information diverge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption of downstream innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: A central policy rationale for §101 exclusions is to avoid claims that preempt future uses and downstream technologies — the 'storehouse of knowledge' concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether the claim would block future inventive activity or practical applications that would otherwise be available to all; heavy preemption risk argues for exclusion or narrowing of claims under §101 (as in Mayo/Alice reasoning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness / inventiveness (§103) as a probe for patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical cases (e.g., Funk Bros., American Fruit Growers) denied patents because the claimed combination or product lacked inventiveness—qualities unchanged from nature suggested no inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the claimed composition is merely an aggregation or packaging of natural components or properties such that it lacks the inventive step under §103; these §103/obviousness considerations were often the real basis of pre-1952 'product-of-nature' rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: §112 disclosure / commensurability as claim-limiting tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure doctrines (§112) and commensurability requirements can limit overly broad product claims and may be more appropriate than a categorical §101 exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where claims are broad or foundational, consider whether specification and claim scope are commensurate; use §112 to constrain claim breadth rather than importing a sweeping §101 rule in every case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building-block / fundamentality metric
rubrics_metrics.description: A product may be excluded if it is an upstream 'building block' essential to follow-on innovation — i.e., too fundamental to be monopolized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claimed composition occupies an upstream, foundational role such that exclusive rights would impede downstream inventive work; the article notes this is a desirable policy goal but warns the metric is hard to apply to products versus processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim breadth, disclosed embodiments, and cumulative-improvement factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentators propose multi-factor tests (claim breadth, number of disclosed embodiments, likelihood of cumulative improvements) to determine whether a claim is 'fundamental' or overbroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these indicia as proxies for preemption risk and ‘fundamentality’; the author recognizes merit in such multi-factor approaches but cautions about their problematic application to material/product claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural-occurrence / inherency test
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claimed composition is naturally occurring or could be fortuitously produced (inherency), that fact can weigh against patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: the universe-wide possibility that any composition might occur naturally undermines a pure natural-occurrence test; the author notes inherency rationale is conceptually troubling as a bright-line rule for §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category distinction: composition-of-matter versus machine/manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: Machines and manufactures carry an implication of human creation; compositions of matter raise different product-of-nature concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate analyses by §101 statutory category: compositions may more readily implicate product-of-nature questions, whereas machines/manufactures are less likely to be characterized as 'of nature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional-attributes versus structural-claims distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts often conflate discussion of a material’s 'qualities' (functional attributes) with the patent claim, but claims typically assert structures, not mere properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating statements about natural qualities as if the patent directly claims those qualities; analyze the claim language to see whether it claims a structure/composition or merely tries to monopolize a property or natural quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: New uses / practical utility of isolated molecules
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical, novel uses to which an isolated material can be put (e.g., genetic testing, primers/probes) may support patent eligibility (Judge Moore’s concurrence reasoning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether isolation enables new, specific, practical applications unavailable in the natural state; novel uses can be evidence of human contribution relevant to eligibility or to novelty/utility inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept requirement (Mayo/Alice step-two) applied to products
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying a 'building-block' or natural product, analyze whether the claim contains an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform it into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the article's critique that it's unclear what constitutes an 'inventive concept' for tangible compositions (unlike specialized hardware/software examples); courts must articulate concrete indicia for product cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removing pre-existing public-domain benefits / inherency-preemption concern
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is problematic when it removes from the public domain something already in common use or confers a monopoly over what others already rely upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether granting the claim would take away public access to prior-benefit materials or methods; doctrines like inherency, on-sale bar, and anticipation are relevant to this evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human synthesis versus extraction (origin of material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a composition is entirely synthetic (never occurs in nature) or is merely extracted/purified from a natural source influences the eligibility analysis (e.g., PNA synthetic polymers vs extracted gDNA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess origin: synthetic constructs that would not occur in nature are more plausibly patent-eligible, though informational equivalence to natural materials complicates the analysis (as with PNA vs gDNA/cDNA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal development and cumulative-progression consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The order in which materials are discovered and applications developed affects the preemption analysis (materials often need to be discovered before applications can be built).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine development timelines: foundational materials discovered early may justify different treatment than abstract principles that govern many existing processes; this temporality should inform whether exclusion is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storehouse-of-knowledge / public-access rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: One normative justification for excluding fundamental compositions is to preserve a public commons of basic building blocks — the 'storehouse of knowledge'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the public-interest in keeping foundational materials unmonopolized against the incentivizing function of patents; the author cautions this rationale is less compelling for compositions than for laws of nature because compositions are less universally antecedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use other doctrinal levers rather than broad §101 exclusions (policy-driven, invention-by-invention approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author suggests the possible need for a more granular, invention-specific policy lever (e.g., refined §112, §103, or guidelines) instead of expansive §101 rejections to police fundamental product claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider tailoring remedies—claim construction, §112 disclosure limits, novelty/obviousness analyses, and specific statutory rules—before resorting to categorical §101 exclusions that are difficult to administrate for products.
